q: Which built-in role lets a user view everything in a subscription but change nothing?
exp: Reader can view every resource and setting within its scope but can't create, change or delete anything, and can't assign roles. Contributor and Owner can change resources, and User Access Administrator can change role assignments.

q: Which types of security principal can receive an Azure role assignment?
opts: Users, groups, service principals, and managed identities
exp: An Azure role can be assigned to four types of security principal: users, groups, service principals (apps) and managed identities. Devices can't receive roles, and subscriptions are scopes, not principals.

q: What is the smallest scope at which you can assign an Azure role?
exp: Azure roles can be assigned at four levels: management group, subscription, resource group, or a single resource. The smallest is an individual resource, such as one storage account or VM.

q: A developer must manage virtual machines in RG-Dev but must NOT be able to manage the virtual network or the storage accounts. Least-privilege role?
exp: Virtual Machine Contributor can create and manage VMs but not the virtual network or storage accounts they connect to (it only gets the join permissions it needs). Contributor on RG-Dev would also allow managing the VNet and storage. Network Contributor is the opposite (networking only), and Owner is far more than needed.

q: An engineer needs to manage VNets, NSGs, and load balancers in a subscription without access to VMs. Which role?
exp: Network Contributor lets you manage networking resources such as virtual networks, subnets, NSGs, load balancers and public IPs, but not VMs or storage. Virtual Machine Contributor is the opposite. Contributor would include VMs, and Security Admin is a Defender for Cloud role.

q: An app needs to read blobs in a storage account using Microsoft Entra authentication. Which role assignment is least privileged?
opts: Storage Blob Data Reader on the container or account
exp: Reading blob contents with Entra authentication needs a data-plane role such as Storage Blob Data Reader, assigned on the container (least privilege) or the account. Reader and Storage Account Contributor are control-plane roles, so they don't grant data access through Entra ID. Owner gives far too much.

q: A finance user must view invoices and billing data but not resources. Which role?
exp: Billing Reader can read billing data such as invoices and cost information, without access to resources. Reader would show all resources. Cost Management Contributor can also change cost settings like budgets, which goes beyond view-only. Owner is full control.

q: A user must view cost data and create budgets but not modify resources. Which role fits best?
exp: Cost Management Contributor can view costs and manage cost settings such as budgets and exports, without changing resources. Contributor can change resources, Reader and Billing Reader can only view, and Billing Reader is for billing data rather than budgets.

q: In the portal, where do you add a role assignment for a resource group?
opts: Resource group → Access control (IAM) → Add role assignment
exp: Every scope (management group, subscription, resource group and resource) has an Access control (IAM) blade, where Add → Add role assignment creates an Azure RBAC assignment. Entra ID → Roles and administrators is for directory roles such as User Administrator, which are a different system.

q: You want to find out what roles a specific user has on a resource group, including inherited ones. Fastest portal tool?
exp: Access control (IAM) → Check access lets you pick a user, group or identity and see every role they have at that scope, including roles inherited from higher scopes and through group membership. The Activity log shows past operations, not current access, and Advisor and Policy don't report RBAC.

q: Which CLI command lists all role assignments for a user, including those inherited from higher scopes?
exp: az role assignment list --assignee lists a principal's role assignments. --all includes every scope in the subscription (not just the subscription itself), and --include-inherited adds assignments inherited from higher scopes such as management groups. The other commands don't exist.

q: Which PowerShell cmdlet assigns a role?
exp: New-AzRoleAssignment creates a role assignment, for example -SignInName, -RoleDefinitionName and -ResourceGroupName. New-AzRoleDefinition creates a custom role (the definition, not the assignment). Add-AzRole and Set-AzRbac don't exist.

q: A subscription reaches its role assignment limit. What's the recommended way to reduce assignments?
opts: Assign roles to groups instead of individual users
exp: A subscription has a limit on role assignments (4,000). Assigning roles to groups means one assignment covers every member, so you use far fewer. Extra subscriptions, deny assignments and Azure Policy don't reduce the number of assignments.

q: User1 is Owner of RG1. An administrator applies a ReadOnly lock to RG1. Can User1 delete a VM in RG1?
opts: No — locks apply to all users regardless of role
exp: Resource locks apply to everyone, whatever role they have — they are a safety net on top of RBAC. While the ReadOnly lock is in place even an Owner can't delete or change resources in RG1. The Owner can remove the lock first (Owners have lock permissions), then delete.

q: Azure RBAC is built on which service?
exp: Azure RBAC is the authorisation system of Azure Resource Manager: every management request goes through ARM, and ARM checks the caller's role assignments before running it. Azure Policy is a separate governance service, Entra Connect syncs identities, and Azure Monitor collects telemetry.

q: User1 has Contributor on Sub1. Which TWO actions can User1 NOT perform?
opts: Create a VM in any resource group of Sub1
Assign the Reader role to User2 on Sub1
Delete a resource group in Sub1
Create a resource lock on a resource group
exp: Contributor has Actions = * but NotActions removes Microsoft.Authorization/*/Write and Delete. Creating role assignments and creating locks are both Microsoft.Authorization write operations, so Contributor can't do them. It can create VMs and delete resource groups, because those are ordinary resource operations.

q: Answer Yes or No to each statement:
stmts: A role can be assigned to a managed identity
Role assignments to a group apply to its members
A Reader at the subscription scope can read resources in every resource group of that subscription
Removing a user from Entra ID automatically deletes their role assignments
exp: Managed identities can receive roles, and a role assigned to a group applies to all its members. Reader at the subscription scope is inherited by every resource group and resource. But deleting a user in Entra ID doesn't remove their role assignments — they stay as 'Identity not found' until you clean them up.

q: After moving a subscription to a different Entra tenant, users from the old tenant can no longer manage resources. Why?
opts: All role assignments are permanently removed when a subscription changes tenant
The subscription is disabled for 30 days
exp: Moving a subscription to a different Microsoft Entra tenant permanently deletes all its Azure RBAC role assignments, because the old tenant's users and groups don't exist in the new one. Resources keep running, but you must recreate the role assignments in the new tenant.

q: What do Azure RBAC 'conditions' (ABAC) allow you to do on top of role assignments?
opts: Add attribute-based checks, for example limiting blob access by blob index tags
Deny all access to a tenant
exp: Role assignment conditions (attribute-based access control) add an extra check to a role assignment, such as 'only blobs with index tag Project=Alpha' or 'only containers named logs'. They make a role narrower. They don't deny the whole tenant, schedule assignments (that's PIM) or enforce MFA (that's Conditional Access).

q: Admins must activate the Owner role only when needed, for a limited time, with approval. Which feature?
opts: Microsoft Entra Privileged Identity Management (eligible assignments)
exp: Privileged Identity Management makes users eligible for a role instead of permanently assigned. They activate it only when needed, for a limited time, optionally with approval, MFA and a justification. It needs Entra ID P2 or ID Governance. Locks, policies and access reviews don't provide just-in-time access.

q: Which built-in role allows managing resource locks and role assignments but not other resources?
exp: User Access Administrator has full rights on Microsoft.Authorization, which covers role assignments and management locks, and no rights on other resources. Contributor manages resources but is explicitly blocked from Microsoft.Authorization writes, so it can't manage locks or access.

q: A role is assigned at the Tenant Root Group management group. What does it cover?
opts: All management groups, subscriptions, and resources in the tenant
Nothing; assignments at root aren't allowed
exp: The tenant root group is the top of the management group hierarchy. A role assigned there is inherited by every management group, subscription, resource group and resource in the tenant. It doesn't cover Entra ID objects, because those use separate Entra roles.

q: Which statement best describes the Owner role?
opts: Full access to manage all resources, including assigning roles in Azure RBAC
exp: Owner has every permission on resources at its scope and can also assign roles to others. That's effectively Contributor plus User Access Administrator. It can delete resources and isn't limited to billing.

q: A user is in Group A (Reader on RG1) and Group B (Contributor on RG1). There is no deny assignment. Effective permission on RG1?
exp: Azure RBAC is additive: a user's effective permissions are the combination (union) of all their role assignments, direct or through groups. Reader plus Contributor on RG1 gives everything Contributor allows. Roles never cancel each other out; only a deny assignment can take permissions away.

q: What happens when a deny assignment conflicts with a role assignment that allows the same action?
opts: The deny assignment wins — deny takes precedence
exp: Deny assignments are evaluated before role assignments. If a deny assignment blocks an action, the user can't do it even if one of their roles allows it. They are created by Azure itself, for example by deployment stacks with deny settings, not added directly by administrators.

q: Which section of a custom role controls data-plane operations such as reading blob contents?
exp: Role definitions separate the control plane from the data plane. Actions and NotActions cover management operations, such as creating a storage account. DataActions and NotDataActions cover operations on the data inside, such as reading or writing blob contents. AssignableScopes says where the role can be assigned.

q: What is the quickest way to create a custom role similar to an existing built-in role in the portal?
opts: IAM → Roles → select a built-in role → Clone
exp: In any scope's Access control (IAM) → Roles, you can pick a built-in role and choose Clone to start a custom role with its permissions already filled in, then add or remove actions. Entra ID → Roles is for directory roles, and policy definitions are a different feature.

q: Which CLI command creates a custom role from a JSON file?
exp: az role definition create --role-definition role.json creates a custom role from a JSON file that contains Name, Actions, NotActions, DataActions and AssignableScopes. az role assignment create only assigns an existing role, and policy definitions are a different feature.

q: Can a custom role use the root scope "/" in AssignableScopes?
opts: No — custom roles can't use root scope; only built-in roles are available there
exp: A custom role's AssignableScopes can list management groups, subscriptions or resource groups, but not the root scope "/". Only built-in roles can be assigned at root. Licences and data actions don't change this.

q: How many management groups can a custom role list in AssignableScopes?
exp: A custom role's AssignableScopes can list several subscriptions and resource groups, but at most one management group. This is a platform limit, so 'unlimited' and 'up to 5' are wrong; management groups are allowed, just only one.

q: A custom role has Actions ["Microsoft.Compute/*"] and NotActions ["Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/delete"]. The user also has Contributor on the same scope. Can they delete a VM?
opts: Yes — NotActions doesn't block permissions granted by another role
No — custom roles override built-in roles
Only if the VM is stopped
exp: NotActions is not a deny. It only removes actions from that one custom role. Because RBAC is additive, the user's Contributor role still includes Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/delete, so the user can delete the VM. Only a deny assignment could block it.

q: What does the wildcard in "Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/*" grant?
opts: All operations on storage accounts and their child control-plane resources
exp: The * wildcard grants every control-plane operation under Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts — create, read, update, delete, list keys and child resources. It doesn't grant data access to blobs; that needs DataActions. It covers only storage accounts, not every resource provider.

q: Which operation string allows a user to start virtual machines?
exp: Starting a VM is an action, so its operation string is Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/start/action. The /write operation creates or updates the VM definition, which is a different permission. Strings like Microsoft.Compute/start or Microsoft.VM/start don't exist.

q: Order the steps to create and use a custom role via CLI:
items: Assign the role with az role assignment create
Write the role definition JSON (Actions, AssignableScopes)
Verify it with az role definition list --custom-role-only
exp: First write the JSON with Name, Actions and AssignableScopes. Then create the role with az role definition create. Check it exists with az role definition list --custom-role-only true. Only then can you assign it with az role assignment create, because a role must exist before it can be assigned.

q: Answer Yes or No about custom roles:
stmts: Custom roles can be shared across subscriptions that trust the same tenant
A custom role can be assigned outside its AssignableScopes
Custom roles require Entra ID P1 or P2
exp: Custom roles are usable within listed scopes in the same tenant; they cannot be assigned outside AssignableScopes; no Entra premium license is needed; DataActions are supported.

q: Which role should a monitoring team get to view metrics and logs and create alert rules, without changing resources?
exp: Monitoring Contributor can read all monitoring data and change monitoring settings such as alert rules and diagnostic settings, without changing the resources themselves. Contributor and Owner give far more access, and Log Analytics Reader can only read data.

q: A user must only read monitoring data such as metrics and logs. Which role?
exp: Monitoring Reader can read all monitoring data — metrics, logs and alert settings — but can't change anything. Monitoring Contributor can also create alerts and change diagnostic settings. Log Analytics Contributor can manage workspaces, which is more than read-only.

q: A backup operator must manage backups (start backup, restore) but not delete backup data or vaults. Which role?
exp: Backup Operator can run backups and restores but cannot remove backup data, create vaults or grant access. Backup Contributor can also manage backup policies and remove backup data.

q: Which role lets a user connect to a VM via Microsoft Entra login with administrator privileges inside the OS?
exp: Entra-based VM login uses Virtual Machine Administrator Login (admin rights in the OS) or Virtual Machine User Login (standard user). VM Contributor doesn't grant OS login.

q: You assign the Reader role to a guest user on RG1. What does the guest see in the Azure portal?
opts: The resources in RG1, after switching to your directory
exp: A guest who is given Reader on RG1 signs in with their own account, switches to your directory in the portal, and sees only the resources in RG1. They don't see other resource groups or the rest of the tenant, because they have no role anywhere else.

ctx: Assignments: User1 — Owner on RG-A. User2 — User Access Administrator on Sub1 (contains RG-A). User3 — Contributor on Sub1.
q: Which users can grant User4 the Reader role on RG-A?
exp: User1 is Owner on RG-A, which includes granting access. User2 is User Access Administrator on Sub1, and that role is inherited by RG-A. User3 is Contributor, which can't create role assignments. So User1 and User2 can grant Reader.

ctx: User1 has Reader on management group MG1 (contains Sub1) and Virtual Machine Contributor on RG-VMs in Sub1.
q: Answer Yes or No:
stmts: User1 can restart a VM in RG-VMs
User1 can create a virtual network in RG-VMs
User1 can view storage accounts in other resource groups of Sub1
User1 can assign Reader to another user on RG-VMs
exp: Virtual Machine Contributor covers VM actions such as restart, but not creating virtual networks. Reader on MG1 is inherited by Sub1, so User1 can view storage accounts in every resource group. Neither role includes roleAssignments/write, so User1 can't assign roles.

q: Where are Microsoft Entra directory roles (like User Administrator) assigned?
exp: Directory roles such as User Administrator or Global Administrator control Entra ID itself and are assigned in Entra ID → Roles and administrators. Access control (IAM) on a subscription assigns Azure RBAC roles for resources. These two role systems are separate.

q: Which Entra role is the most privileged and should be assigned to as few people as possible?
exp: Global Administrator has full access to every part of Microsoft Entra ID and the services that use it. Microsoft recommends fewer than five Global Administrators and using less-privileged roles, such as User Administrator, for day-to-day work.

q: Can a group be assigned a Microsoft Entra directory role?
opts: Yes, if the group was created as role-assignable (isAssignableToRole = true)
exp: Groups can receive Entra directory roles only if they're created as role-assignable (isAssignableToRole = true). That setting is chosen at creation and can't be changed later, and role-assignable groups can't use dynamic membership. Ordinary groups can't be given Entra roles.

q: A user needs to manage app registrations and enterprise applications only. Least-privilege Entra role?
exp: Application Administrator can create and manage app registrations and enterprise applications, including their single sign-on and proxy settings, without broader directory rights. Global Administrator would be far too much, User Administrator manages users and groups, and Cloud Device Administrator manages devices.

q: A VM-hosted app must access Key Vault without storing credentials in code. What should you use?
opts: A managed identity for the VM, granted access to Key Vault
A user's password in app settings
exp: A managed identity gives the VM an identity in Entra ID that Azure manages, with no secrets in code. Grant that identity access to Key Vault (an RBAC role or access policy), and the app gets tokens from the VM's local endpoint. Keys, passwords and SAS tokens would all have to be stored somewhere.

q: Five VMs need the SAME identity with the same permissions, and the identity must survive if a VM is deleted. Which type?
exp: User-assigned identities are standalone resources, can be shared across resources, and have an independent lifecycle. System-assigned identities are deleted with their resource.

q: What happens to a system-assigned managed identity when its VM is deleted?
exp: A system-assigned managed identity is created with its resource and shares its lifecycle, so deleting the VM deletes the identity and its role assignments stop working. If you need an identity that outlives the resource or is shared by several resources, use a user-assigned identity.

q: Order the steps so a web app can read secrets from Key Vault (RBAC permission model) without credentials:
items: Assign 'Key Vault Secrets User' to the identity on the vault
Enable a system-assigned managed identity on the web app
Reference the secret from the app using its identity
Confirm the vault uses the Azure RBAC permission model
exp: First enable the web app's managed identity, so there's an identity to grant access to. Confirm the vault uses the Azure RBAC permission model, then assign Key Vault Secrets User to the identity. Finally reference the secret from the app, which reads it using the identity — no credentials needed.
